record.tranche_reason: The study uses transcoder feature circuits and interventions in LLMs, reporting whether sparse dictionary features are recoverable and causally relevant. This bears on V4, but it does not test the original toy-model superposition setup.
record.gate_note: The paper discusses sparse features and polysemanticity as background and uses transcoders to analyze planning. It does not test feature overlap, superposition geometry, or neuron polysemanticity as capacity competition. Results about planning are included only where they directly demonstrate recovered transcoder features or their interventions; unrelated planning-task metrics are omitted.
record.test_reason: The paper uses per-layer transcoders (163,840 features, from Hanna et al. 2025) to study latent planning in Qwen-3. Superposition and polysemanticity appear only as background motivation for using sparse dictionaries (Sec. 3, App. A.1). All results measure whether planning features are present and causally drive a/an, is/are, el/la, rhyme and measure-word outputs. None measures whether a dictionary recovers the model's features, how features spread across neurons, superposition geometry, or dictionary completeness or stability. The record's V4 'supports' rests on the tool working for the paper's own purpose, which is T4 use, not a test.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. More precisely: Qwen-3 models show latent planning that grows with scale. Planning features represent planned words and causally shape both the word and the preceding context (a/an, is/are). Forward planning develops before backward planning, and even 14B rarely plans multiple tokens ahead. The paper draws no conclusions about superposition.
record.recipe_differences: The original source studies toy models of superposition; this paper analyzes Qwen-3 language models with per-layer transcoders, feature circuits, and feature interventions to study latent planning.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported feature availability and intervention effects vary by task and model scale; the paper also says local-planning results are sensitive to steering strength.

fits_no_version.finding: Authors speculate transcoders may miss higher-number features in is/are. The rhyme-feature heuristic has moderate recall. Direct-effect interventions in the Chinese task are used to infer features hidden in transcoder error.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Per-layer transcoder dictionaries may miss task-relevant features (dictionary incompleteness); suggested, not measured.

record.problems: The study covers one model family. Feature labels and circuit interpretations include qualitative/manual analysis; rhyme-feature recovery is described as high precision but moderate recall. The authors note that transcoders may miss features, and direct-effects interventions are weaker than full interventions.
record.rows_left_out: Not applicable. Planning-task behavioral rates, probes, and other circuit interventions were excluded unless they specifically demonstrated sparse transcoder-feature recovery or its causal effects.

untested.parts: All: no toy models, no geometry, no sparsity transition.
All: capacity competition is cited as background only (App. A.1), not tested.
All: no analysis of causes of polysemantic neurons.
All: transcoders are assumed to recover monosemantic features. No measure of feature spread across neurons or dictionary recovery quality.
All: no test of completeness, stability or canonicity of dictionary features.
All: no test of feature dimensionality. Separate vowel and consonant rhyme features are noted only descriptively.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked planning-intervention rows to V4 because transcoder features were usable. This is tool use (T4). All rows are relinked to none, and the V4 labels are dropped.

versions.untested_parts: Toy networks, feature overlap and near-orthogonal geometry, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometric arrangements.
Whether neuron polysemanticity results from capacity competition or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Alternative causes of polysemantic neurons and whether polysemanticity is evidence of superposition.
The study uses transcoders, not SAEs, and does not measure how features are distributed across neurons.
Whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units of model representation.
Whether the represented features are intrinsically one-dimensional rather than multidimensional.

rows.subject: Qwen-3 (14B)
rows.operation_detail: Inspected transcoder feature circuits for the a/an task.
rows.measure: Whether interpretable transcoder features represent a planned word and contribute to the next-token output
rows.value: The circuit contains features representing accountant that feed into features increasing the planned word and the appropriate article.
rows.note: A qualitative circuit example; the authors say similar planning features occur in their analyses.
rows.check: Qualitative planning-circuit example (Fig. 1). It shows transcoder features used as a tool, not a test of whether sparse features exist or are recovered.

rows.subject: Qwen-3 4B
rows.operation_detail: Zeroed selected planning-feature activations on examples the model answered correctly.
rows.value: Ablating planning features harms performance on minority-class an examples.
rows.note: The paper says these interventions are effective on Qwen-3 4B and 8B; effects are concentrated on an examples.
rows.check: Ablation of planning features on a/an measures planning causality, not superposition or dictionary recovery. The subject is listed as 4B only, but Fig. 3 covers all five models (0.6B–14B); the text says ablation harms only 'an' examples.

rows.subject: Qwen-3 8B
rows.operation_detail: Set selected planning-feature activations to 5× their usual activations on examples the model initially answered incorrectly.
rows.value: Boosting planning features improves performance on an examples; the authors describe the improvement as drastic.
rows.note: The intervention is feature-specific and is more successful than the random-feature baseline.
rows.check: 5× boosting of planning features is a planning-mechanism result, not a test of V4. Fig. 3 covers all models, not only 8B. The stated random-feature baseline (App. F) is the study's own control.

rows.subject: Qwen-3 0.6B–14B models
rows.operation_detail: Identified planning-relevant features in transcoder circuits across the a/an, is/are, and el/la tasks.
rows.measure: Presence and task relevance of interpretable transcoder features
rows.value: The authors report planning-relevant features in these task circuits, but say features are less common in el/la; they also note that transcoder misses may explain some absent features.
rows.note: The text reports the cross-model pattern qualitatively rather than giving a single aggregate rate.
rows.check: Presence of planning features per task concerns planning. The remark that transcoders may miss number features is speculative ('unclear') and is not measured.

rows.subject: Qwen-3 models (0.6B–14B; larger models identified as 8B–14B)
rows.operation_detail: Downweighted original rhyme features and upweighted features associated with a different rhyme.

conditions.value: original rhyme features × -3; replacement rhyme features × 7

rows.measure: Accuracy of producing the steered rhyme
rows.baseline: Normal rhyming accuracy was about 60%; assonant rhyme accuracy was higher, up to 60% in the steered condition.
rows.value: For larger models (8B–14B), steering changes the rhyme with about 40% accuracy; the authors describe the result as moderate.
rows.note: The text reports the larger-model range collectively; it does not give a separate exact value for each model in prose.
rows.check: Rhyme steering accuracy (~40% for 8B–14B) measures forward planning. The baseline field mixes unsteered rhyme accuracy (~60%) with steered assonant accuracy.

rows.subject: Qwen-3 models (0.6B–14B)
rows.operation_detail: Downweighted planning features from a target example and upweighted features from a source example to replace Chinese measure-word outputs.
rows.measure: Percentage of interventions matching the target example's original measure word
rows.value: The reported match rate increases from 20% to 52.2% with model scale.
rows.note: The study reports a scaling range rather than per-model values in prose; direct-effects interventions are around half as effective.
rows.check: Chinese measure-word replacement (20% to 52.2% match) measures planning control, not superposition. There are only 10 examples.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
